clue.text: Time of raw inexperience?

parts.note: read literally, a period spent eating uncooked greens; really, the green, untested days of youth

explanation.surface: A wistful question about the period when one knew nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra: 'My salad days, when I was green in judgment'. 'Raw' hints at uncooked salad leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a youthful period of naivety, when one was green like lettuce.

clue.text: Father and son writing up about first of Grecians — or his character?

indicators.note: about means the reversed name goes around the letter taken from the Greek word
in a down clue, up means the name is written from bottom to top

parts.note: Kingsley and Martin Amis were a father and son who were both novelists

indicators.note: first of means only the opening letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: A father and son of letters write about a Greek, or perhaps about his personality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses AMIS to SIMA, and 'about' puts G around it.
explanation.definitionFit: A Greek's character can be a letter of his alphabet, and the eighteenth letter of the Greek alphabet is one.

clue.text: One cleaning up filthy habits

parts.note: on the surface a reformer of dirty ways; really someone who washes dirty clothes, or makes dirty money look clean

explanation.surface: A moral crusader sets out to reform people's disgusting ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habits' are also clothes, as in a monk's habit, and 'filthy' money is what gets made to look legitimate.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who washes and irons clothes, or passes dirty money through clean channels, does this job.

clue.text: Parent beset by dirtiest sort of skin condition

indicators.note: beset by means the parent word is surrounded by the other letters
sort of suggests a rearranged version, so the letters of the word are mixed

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother, a parent

explanation.surface: A mother surrounded by grime suffers a skin complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges DIRTIEST, and 'beset by' puts those letters around MA.
explanation.definitionFit: This is inflammation of the skin, a general medical term for an irritated rash.

clue.text: Wanted, like good wine

parts.note: as means like, in comparisons
pi is short for pious, good in a religious sense
red is a colour of wine

explanation.surface: A good wine is in demand.
explanation.walkthrough: PI is crossword shorthand for pious, hence good.
explanation.definitionFit: To aspire to something is to aim at or long for it.

clue.text: Placate small, small figure

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as in clothing sizes
wee is Scottish for small
ten is a number, a figure

explanation.surface: Someone tries to calm a small, small figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Repeating 'small' looks like a typo for emphasis; it supplies two different pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To make someone more amenable or less angry is to mollify them.

clue.text: Cedar's top branch — how do you get there?

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter, so only the start of the tree's name is used

parts.note: a branch of a tree is a limb

explanation.surface: Someone eyeing the highest bough of a cedar asks how to reach it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads back over the surface: to reach the top branch you must ascend.
explanation.definitionFit: Going up something, such as a tree, is how one reaches a high place.

clue.text: Bird observes its predator swallowing hard

indicators.note: swallowing means the predator word takes the letter for hard inside it

parts.note: a cat preys on birds
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A bird watches a cat gulping something down.
explanation.walkthrough: A CHAT is a small songbird such as the stonechat or whinchat.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a small songbird of the thrush family, like the stonechat.

clue.text: See 25
Aim to enter trade as local worker

indicators.note: to enter means the aim word goes inside the trade word

parts.note: to barter is to trade goods
an end is an aim or goal

explanation.surface: Someone sets out to go into business as a worker in the area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' is British for the pub one regularly visits, so the worker serves drinks there.
explanation.definitionFit: A British local is a neighbourhood pub, and the person serving behind its bar works there.

clue.text: One sticking trees up, logs turned evenly

indicators.note: turned means the letters picked out are then read backwards
evenly means taking the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on of the run of words

explanation.surface: A lumberjack is pictured sticking trees upright and turning logs over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'evenly' picks R, E, U, L, G from 'trees up, logs'; 'turned' reverses them.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who sticks things together with adhesive is a person who applies glue.

clue.text: Poor writer, one sampling author?

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe was an American author of tales and verse
someone who samples food or wine is a taster

explanation.surface: A reviewer dismisses a bad writer as someone who merely dabbles in another author's work.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetaster is an inferior versifier, a writer of trashy poetry.

clue.text: See 22
Man getting on in the Guardian?

parts.note: a man is referred to as he
re means on or concerning, as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a man getting on in years appears in the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle was printed in the Guardian, so from where the reader sits 'in the Guardian' is this very place.
explanation.definitionFit: For a reader of this newspaper, being in the paper means being in this place, the present location.

clue.text: Golfer's unspecific requirement from caddie in song

definitions.text: Golfer's unspecific requirement from caddie in song

parts.words: Golfer's unspecific requirement from caddie in song
parts.note: a golfer who does not care which club the caddie hands over would ask for any metal-headed one; the phrase is also a song title

explanation.surface: A golfer who isn't fussy about clubs asks the caddie for whatever comes to hand.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf an iron is a type of club. ANY OLD IRON is a British music hall song made famous by Harry Champion.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both a careless request for a golf club and the title of a music hall song.

clue.text: See 25
Keeping under wraps?

parts.note: normally means keeping secret; read literally, preserved inside bandages, as an embalmed body in Egypt

explanation.surface: Something is being kept secret.
explanation.walkthrough: Ancient Egyptians preserved bodies by embalming them and wrapping them in linen bandages.
explanation.definitionFit: An embalmed body wrapped in bandages is preserved under wraps in the most literal way.

clue.text: Gesture of acknowledgement about new slipper, not for slipping on

indicators.note: about means the gesture word goes around the other pieces

parts.note: a nod of the head acknowledges someone
a ski slips over snow, so it is a slipper

explanation.surface: Someone nods in acknowledgement at a new slipper with a grippy sole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slipper' looks like footwear, but here it is something that slips: a ski.
explanation.definitionFit: A non-skid surface is designed so that it does not slip under one's feet.

clue.text: Equipment then is modified, so lively

parts.note: kit is equipment

indicators.note: modified means the letters of the words before it are changed around

explanation.surface: Some gear is altered and becomes more energetic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'modified' rearranges THEN IS into TENISH.
explanation.definitionFit: Being playful and frisky, like a young cat, means being sprightly.

clue.text: See 25
Sensitive area where sticky stuff is situated

parts.note: goo is sticky stuff
something that lies somewhere is situated there

explanation.surface: A tender spot is where something gooey has been placed.
explanation.walkthrough: GOOLIES is British slang for the testicles.
explanation.definitionFit: This British slang word means the testicles, a notoriously tender part of the body.

clue.text: Fish left in hat

indicators.note: in means the letter for left is placed inside the hat word

parts.note: a boater is a flat straw hat

explanation.surface: A fish has been left inside someone's hat.
explanation.walkthrough: A BOATER is a stiff straw hat with a flat top, traditionally worn for summer boating.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloater is a herring cured by salting and smoking whole.

clue.text: European city created stink detailing African nation's uprising

parts.note: BO, body odour, is a stink

indicators.note: in a down clue, uprising means the shortened country is written upwards
detailing means taking the tail, or last letter, off the country

parts.note: Angola is a nation in southern Africa

explanation.surface: An uprising in an African nation creates a stink in a European city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailing' cuts ANGOLA to ANGOL; 'uprising' reverses it to LOGNA.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a city in northern Italy, capital of Emilia-Romagna.

clue.text: Second (not leader), second-rate

indicators.note: not leader means the word for a brief moment loses its first letter

parts.note: a second, a very short time, is a jiffy

explanation.surface: Something not quite first is dismissed as inferior.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, something dubious or of poor quality is described as dodgy or doubtful.

clue.text: Dickens's character preparing to light up?

definitions.meaning: the old thief who runs a gang of boys in Oliver Twist
read as two words, a fag (British slang for cigarette) in the mouth, ready to smoke

explanation.walkthrough: Fag is British slang for a cigarette, so with a fag in one's mouth one is ready to light up.
explanation.definitionFit: The criminal mentor of the pickpockets in Oliver Twist; split, it describes a cigarette ready to smoke.

clue.text: Squeakless apiarist Washington, entering pub, goes off to find song

indicators.note: entering means the first pieces go inside the pub word

parts.note: a bar is a pub
a hinge that has been oiled no longer squeaks
an apiarist keeps bees, so is a bee fan
DC, the District of Columbia, is Washington
food that goes off rots

explanation.surface: A silent beekeeper from Washington walks into a pub and leaves to look for a tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squeakless' gives OILED, as a hinge that has been oiled stops squeaking. BOILED BEEF AND CARROTS is a 1909 British music hall song made famous by Harry Champion.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the title of an old comic music hall number, so it is a song.

clue.text: Thinner is better

explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of fine covers both slenderer and of higher quality.

clue.text: Rope of execution?

definitions.meaning: a strong rope supporting a ship's mast
completes the phrase for a postponement of a death sentence

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a fill-in: the word goes before 'of execution'. 'Rope' and 'execution' together suggest the hangman.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's supporting rope; also a postponement, as in the stock phrase for halting an execution.

clue.text: Unfortunately, third time minimum having lost, um, engagement ring, one containing gold — so get me to the church on time!

definitions.text: so get me to the church on time!

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things gone wrong, so the letters are thrown into disorder
having lost means the two letters given are taken out of the preceding word

parts.note: I, the Roman numeral, stands for one
or is the heraldic term for gold

explanation.surface: A third failed engagement leaves a ring with gold in it, and a groom desperate to be on time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having lost' takes UM from MINIMUM, leaving MINIM. 'Unfortunately' shuffles THIRD, T, MINIM, ENGAGEMENT, RING, I and OR. The answer and the definition are lines from My Fair Lady's song Get Me to the Church on Time.
explanation.definitionFit: In the musical the line is followed by the plea to be taken to the church punctually, so the two phrases belong together.

clue.text: Good to be in control — for its duration?

indicators.note: to be in means the letter for good is placed inside the control word

parts.note: to rein something in is to control it, and reins give control

explanation.surface: Being in control is good, at least while it lasts.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on 'control' before it: the duration of a monarch's control is a period of rule.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch's period of rule lasts as long as their power does, so it is that time span.

clue.text: Small and neat, old penny black

parts.note: D was the abbreviation for a penny in pre-decimal British money
inky means as black as ink

explanation.surface: An old penny is described as compact, tidy and black.
explanation.walkthrough: D stood for the penny in British money before 1971 (from Latin denarius).
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage, dainty and attractively small things are described with this word.

clue.text: So Arachne spinning something to lie to?

indicators.note: spinning suggests turning things around, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Arachne the mythical spider is spinning, perhaps to lie to someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lie to' looks like telling fibs; at sea, a ship lies to when it stays almost still facing the wind, helped by a drogue.
explanation.definitionFit: A drogue dropped overboard keeps a vessel head to wind, so it is what a ship lies to.
